entries.63969558de4d78806fc848f36002f36f598df9f8: <div sID="gen13441" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Prov.5" sID="Prov.5"/> <div eID="gen13441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13442" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> The scope of this chapter is much the same with that of <reference osisRef="Prov.2.1-Prov.2.22">ch. ii</reference>. To write the same things, in other words, ought not to be grievous, for it is safe, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>. Here is, I. An exhortation to get acquaintance with and submit to the laws of wisdom in general, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. A particular caution against the sin of whoredom, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.3-Prov.5.14">ver. 3-14</reference>. III. Remedies prescribed against that sin. 1. Conjugal love, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.15-Prov.5.20">ver. 15-20</reference>. 2. A regard to God's omniscience, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">ver. 21</reference>. 3. A dread of the miserable end of wicked people, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22-Prov.5.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>. And all little enough to arm young people against those fleshly lusts which war against the soul.
entries.686073e8c87b3e3ba8986e68ea90874ad7d5966d: <div eID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13442" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Parental Instructions; Cautions against Sensuality.</title> <div sID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My son, attend unto my wisdom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> bow thine ear to my understanding: <hi type="super">2</hi> That thou mayest regard discretion, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> thy lips may keep knowledge. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the lips of a strange woman drop <hi type="italic">as</hi> an honeycomb, and her mouth <hi type="italic">is</hi> smoother than oil: <hi type="super">4</hi> But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword. <hi type="super">5</hi> Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell. <hi type="super">6</hi> Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou canst not know <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> Hear me now therefore, O ye children, and depart not from the words of my mouth. <hi type="super">8</hi> Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house: <hi type="super">9</hi> Lest thou give thine honour unto others, and thy years unto the cruel: <hi type="super">10</hi> Lest strangers be filled with thy wealth; and thy labours <hi type="italic">be</hi> in the house of a stranger; <hi type="super">11</hi> And thou mourn at the last, when thy flesh and thy body are consumed, <hi type="super">12</hi> And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof; <hi type="super">13</hi> And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined mine ear to them that instructed me! <hi type="super">14</hi> I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation and assembly. <div eID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> I. A solemn preface, to introduce the caution which follows, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.1-Prov.5.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Solomon here addresses himself to his son, that is, to all young men, as unto his children, whom he has an affection for and some influence upon. In God's name, he demands attention; for he writes by divine inspiration, and is a prophet, though he begins not with, <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord. "Attend, and bow thy ear;</hi> not only hear what is said, and read what is written, but apply thy mind to it and consider it diligently." To gain attention he urges, 1. The excellency of his discourse: "It is <hi type="italic">my wisdom, my understanding;</hi> if I undertake to teach thee wisdom I cannot prescribe any thing to be more properly called so; moral philosophy is my philosophy, and that which is to be learned in my school." 2. The usefulness of it: "Attend to what I say," (1.) "That thou mayest act wisely—<hi type="italic">that thou mayest regard discretion.</hi>" Solomon's lectures are not designed to fill our heads with notions, with matters of nice speculation, or doubtful disputation, but to guide us in the government of ourselves, that we may act prudently, so as becomes us and so as will be for our true interest. (2.) "That thou mayest speak wisely—<hi type="italic">that thy lips may keep knowledge,</hi> and thou mayest have it ready at thy tongue's end" (as we say), "for the benefit of those with whom thou dost converse." The priest's lips are said to <hi type="italic">keep knowledge</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal. ii. 7</reference>); but those that are ready and mighty in the scriptures may not only in their devotions, but in their discourses, be spiritual priests. <div eID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> II. The caution itself, and that is to abstain from fleshly lusts, from adultery, fornication, and all uncleanness. Some apply this figuratively, and by the adulterous woman here understand idolatry, or false doctrine, which tends to debauch men's minds and manners, or the sensual appetite, to which it may as fitly as any thing be applied; but the primary scope of it is plainly to warn us against seventh-commandment sins, which youth is so prone to, the temptations to which are so violent, the examples of which are so many, and which, where admitted, are so destructive to all the seeds of virtue in the soul that it is not strange that Solomon's cautions against it are so very pressing and so often repeated. Solomon here, as a faithful watchman, gives fair warning to all, as they regard their lives and comforts, to dread this sin, for it will certainly be their ruin. Two things we are here warned to take heed of:— <div eID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13448" type="x-p"/> 1. That we do not listen to the charms of this sin. It is true <hi type="italic">the lips of a strange woman drop as a honey-comb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.3">v. 3</reference>); the pleasures of fleshly lust are very tempting (like the wine that <hi type="italic">gives its colour in the cup</hi> and <hi type="italic">moves itself aright</hi>); its mouth, the kisses of its mouth, the words of its mouth, are <hi type="italic">smoother than oil,</hi> that the poisonous pill may go down glibly and there may be no suspicion of harm in it. But consider, (1.) How fatal the consequences will be. What fruit will the sinner have of his honey and oil when the end will be, [1.] The terrors of conscience: It <hi type="italic">is bitter as wormwood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">v. 4</reference>. What was luscious in the mouth rises in the stomach and turns sour there; it cuts, in the reflection, like <hi type="italic">a two-edged sword;</hi> take it which way you will, it wounds. Solomon could speak by experience, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Eccl. vii. 26</reference>. [2.] The torments of hell. If some that have been guilty of this sin have repented and been saved, yet the direct tendency of the sin is to destruction of body and soul; the <hi type="italic">feet</hi> of it <hi type="italic">go down to death,</hi> nay, they <hi type="italic">take hold on hell,</hi> to pull it to the sinner, as if the damnations slumbered too long, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">v. 4</reference>. Those that are entangled in this sin should be reminded that there is but a step between them and hell, and that they are ready to drop into it. (2.) Consider how false the charms are. The adulteress flatters and speaks fair, her words are honey and oil, but she will deceive those that hearken to her: <hi type="italic">Her ways are movable, that thou canst not know them;</hi> she often changes her disguise, and puts on a great variety of false colours, because, if she be rightly known, she is certainly hated. Proteus-like, she puts on many shapes, that she may keep in with those whom she has a design upon. And what does she aim at with all this art and management? Nothing but to keep them from <hi type="italic">pondering the path of life,</hi> for she knows that, if they once come to do that, she shall certainly lose them. Those are <hi type="italic">ignorant of Satan's devices</hi> who do not understand that the great thing he drives at in all his temptations is, [1.] To keep them from choosing the path of life, to prevent them from being religious and from going to heaven, that, being himself shut out from happiness, he may keep them out from it. [2.] In order hereunto, to keep them from pondering the path of life, from considering how reasonable it is that they should walk in that path, and how much it will be for their advantage. Be it observed, to the honour of religion, that it certainly gains its point with all those that will but allow themselves the liberty of a serious thought and will weigh things impartially in an even balance, and that the devil has no way of securing men in his interests but by diverting them with continual amusements of one kind or another from the calm and sober consideration of the <hi type="italic">things that belong to their peace.</hi> And uncleanness is a sin that does as much as any thing blind the understanding, sear the conscience, and keep people from pondering the path of life. Whoredom <hi type="italic">takes away the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.4.11">Hos. iv. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen13448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> 2. That we do not approach the borders of this sin, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.7-Prov.5.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> (1.) This caution is introduced with a solemn preface: "<hi type="italic">Hear me now therefore, O you children!</hi> whoever you are that read or hear these lines, take notice of what I say, and mix faith with it, treasure it up, and <hi type="italic">depart not from the words of my mouth,</hi> as those will do that hearken to the words of the strange woman. Do not only receive what I say, for the present merely, but cleave to it, and let it be ready to thee, and of force with thee, when thou art most violently assaulted by the temptation." <div eID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> (2.) The caution itself is very pressing: "<hi type="italic">Remove thy way far from her;</hi> if thy way should happen to lie near her, and thou shouldst have a fair pretence of being led by business within the reach of her charms, yet change thy way, and alter the course of it, rather than expose thyself to danger; <hi type="italic">come not nigh the door of her house;</hi> go on the other side of the street, nay, go through some other street, though it be about." This intimates, [1.] That we ought to have a very great dread and detestation of the sin. We must fear it as we would a place infected with the plague; we must loathe it as the odour of carrion, that we will not come near. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we are likely to preserve our purity when we conceive a rooted antipathy to all fleshly lusts. [2.] That we ought industriously to avoid every thing that may be an occasion of this sin or a step towards it. Those that would be kept from harm must keep out of harm's way. Such tinder there is in the corrupt nature that it is madness, upon any pretence whatsoever, to come near the sparks. If we thrust ourselves into temptation, we mocked God when we prayed, <hi type="italic">Lead us not into temptation.</hi> [3.] That we ought to be jealous over ourselves with a godly jealousy, and not to be so confident of the strength of our own resolutions as to venture upon the brink of sin, with a promise to ourselves that <hi type="italic">hitherto we will come and no further.</hi> [4.] That whatever has become a snare to us and an occasion of sin, though it be as a <hi type="italic">right eye</hi> and a <hi type="italic">right hand,</hi> we must <hi type="italic">pluck it out, cut it off, and cast it from us,</hi> must part with that which is dearest to us rather than hazard our own souls; this is our Saviour's command, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28-Matt.5.30">Matt. v. 28-30</reference>. <div eID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> (3.) The arguments which Solomon here uses to enforce this caution are taken from the same topic with those before, the many mischiefs which attend this sin. [1.] It blasts the reputation. "Thou wilt <hi type="italic">give thy honour unto others</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.9">v. 9</reference>); thou wilt lose it thyself; thou wilt put into the hand of each of thy neighbours a stone to throw at thee, for they will all, with good reason, cry shame on thee, will despise thee, and trample on thee, as a foolish men." Whoredom is a sin that makes men contemptible and base, and no man of sense or virtue will care to keep company with one that keeps company with harlots. [2.] It wastes the time, gives <hi type="italic">the years,</hi> the years of youth, the flower of men's time, <hi type="italic">unto the cruel,</hi> "that base lust of thine, which with the utmost cruelty <hi type="italic">wars against the soul,</hi> that base harlot which pretends an affection for thee, but really hunts for the precious life." Those years that should be given to the honour of a gracious God are spent in the service of a cruel sin. [3.] It ruins the estate (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Strangers</hi> will be <hi type="italic">filled with thy wealth,</hi> which thou art but entrusted with as a steward for thy family; and the fruit of <hi type="italic">thy labours,</hi> which should be provision for thy own house, will be in <hi type="italic">the house of a stranger,</hi> that neither has right to it nor will ever thank thee for it." [4.] It is destructive to the health, and shortens men's days: <hi type="italic">Thy flesh and thy body</hi> will be <hi type="italic">consumed</hi> by it, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">v. 11</reference>. The lusts of uncleanness not only <hi type="italic">war against the soul,</hi> which the sinner neglects and is in no care about, but they war against the body too, which he is so indulgent of and is in such care to please and pamper, such deceitful, such foolish, such hurtful lusts are they. Those that give themselves to work uncleanness with greediness waste their strength, throw themselves into weakness, and often have their bodies filled with loathsome distempers, by which the number of their months is cut off in the midst and they fall unpitied sacrifices to a cruel lust. [5.] It will fill the mind with horror, if ever conscience be awakened. "Though thou art merry now, <hi type="italic">sporting thyself in thy own deceivings,</hi> yet thou wilt certainly <hi type="italic">mourn at the last,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">v. 11</reference>. Thou art all this while making work for repentance, and laying up matter for vexation and torment in the reflection, when the sin is set before thee in its own colours." Sooner or later it will bring sorrow, either when the soul is humbled and brought to repentance or when the <hi type="italic">flesh and body are consumed,</hi> either by sickness, when conscience flies in the sinner's face, or by the grave; when the body is rotting there, the soul is racking in the torments of hell, where the worm dies not, and "<hi type="italic">Son, remember,</hi>" is the constant peal. Solomon here brings in the convinced sinner reproaching himself, and aggravating his own folly. He will then most bitterly lament it. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That because he hated to be reformed he therefore hated to be informed, and could not endure either to be taught his duty (<hi type="italic">How have I hated</hi> not only the discipline of being instructed, but the <hi type="italic">instruction</hi> itself, though all true and good!) or to be told of his faults—<hi type="italic">My heart despised reproof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.12">v. 12</reference>. He cannot but own that those who had the charge of him, parents, ministers, had done their part; they had been his teachers; they had instructed him, had given him good counsel and fair warning (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.13">v. 13</reference>); but to his own shame and confusion does he speak it, and therein justifies God in all the miseries that were brought upon him, he had not <hi type="italic">obeyed their voice,</hi> for indeed he <hi type="italic">never inclined his ear to those that instructed him,</hi> never minded what they said nor admitted the impressions of it. Note, Those who have had a good education and do not live up to it will have a great deal to answer for another day; and those who will not now remember what they were taught, to conform themselves to it, will be made to remember it as an aggravation of their sin, and consequently of their ruin. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That by the frequent acts of sin the habits of it were so rooted and confirmed that his heart was fully set in him to commit it (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation and assembly.</hi> When he came into the synagogue, or into the courts of the temple, to worship God with other Israelites, his unclean heart was full of wanton thoughts and desires and his eyes of adultery. Reverence of the place and company, and of the work that was doing, could not restrain him, but he was almost as wicked and vile there as any where. No sin will appear more frightful to an awakened conscience than the profanation of holy things; nor will any aggravation of sin render it more exceedingly sinful than the place we are honoured with in the congregation and assembly, and the advantages we enjoy thereby. Zimri and Cozbi avowed their villany <hi type="italic">in the sight of Moses and all the congregation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.25.6">Num. xxv. 6</reference>), and heart-adultery is as open to God, and must needs be most offensive to him, when we draw nigh to him in religious exercises. <hi type="italic">I was in all evil</hi> in defiance of the magistrates and judges, and their assemblies; so some understand it. Others refer it to the evil of punishment, not to the evil of sin: "I was made an example, a spectacle to the world. I was under almost all God's sore judgments <hi type="italic">in the midst of the congregation of Israel,</hi> set up for a mark. <hi type="italic">I stood up and cried in the congregation,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.30.28">Job xxx. 28</reference>. Let that be avoided which will be thus rued at last.
entries.382bab6ad7a9132963311b390d242c01f4756ea3: <div eID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conjugal Fidelity Enjoined.</title> <div sID="gen13453" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well. <hi type="super">16</hi> Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad, <hi type="italic">and</hi> rivers of waters in the streets. 17 Let them be only thine own, and not strangers' with thee. 18 Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">Let her be as</hi> the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love. <hi type="super">20</hi> And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger? <hi type="super">21</hi> For the ways of man <hi type="italic">are</hi> before the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he pondereth all his goings. <hi type="super">22</hi> His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins. <hi type="super">23</hi> He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall go astray. <div eID="gen13453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having shown the great evil that there is in adultery and fornication, and all such lewd and filthy courses, here prescribes remedies against them. <div eID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> I. Enjoy with satisfaction the comforts of lawful marriage, which was ordained for the prevention of uncleanness, and therefore ought to be made use of in time, lest it should not prove effectual for the cure of that which it might have prevented. Let none complain that God has dealt unkindly with them in forbidding them those pleasures which they have a natural desire of, for he has graciously provided for the regular gratification of them. "Thou mayest not indeed eat of every tree of the garden, but choose thee out one, which thou pleasest, and of that thou mayest freely eat; nature will be content with that, but lust with nothing." God, in thus confining men to one, has been so far from putting any hardship upon them that he has really consulted their true interest; for, as Mr. Herbert observes, "<hi type="italic">If God had laid all common, certainly man would have been the encloser.</hi>"—Church-porch. Solomon here enlarges much upon this, not only prescribing it as an antidote, but urging it as an argument against fornication, that the allowed pleasures of marriage (however wicked wits may ridicule them, who are factors for the unclean spirit) far transcend all the false forbidden pleasures of whoredom. <div eID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> 1. Let young men marry, marry and not burn. Have <hi type="italic">a cistern,</hi> a <hi type="italic">well of thy own</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.15">v. 15</reference>), even the wife <hi type="italic">of thy youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Wholly abstain, or wed.</hi>—Herbert. "The world is wide, and there are varieties of accomplishments, among which thou mayest please thyself." <div eID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> 2. Let him that is married take delight in his wife, and let him be very fond of her, not only because she is the wife that he himself has chosen and he ought to be pleased with his own choice, but because she is the wife that God in his providence appointed for him and he ought much more to be pleased with the divine appointment, pleased with her because she is his own. <hi type="italic">Let thy fountain be blessed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.18">v. 18</reference>); think thyself very happy in her, look upon her as a blessed wife, let her have thy blessing, pray daily for her, and then <hi type="italic">rejoice with her.</hi> Those comforts we are likely to have joy of that are sanctified to us by prayer and the blessing of God. It is not only allowed us, but commanded us, to be pleasant with our relations; and it particularly becomes yoke-fellows to rejoice together and in each other. Mutual delight is the bond of mutual fidelity. It is not only taken for granted that the <hi type="italic">bridegroom rejoices over his bride</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Isa. lxii. 5</reference>), but given for law. <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.9">Eccl. ix. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of thy life.</hi> Those take not their comforts where God has appointed who are jovial and merry with their companions abroad, but sour and morose with their families at home. <div eID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13458" type="x-p"/> 3. Let him be fond of his wife and love her dearly (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let her be as the loving hind and the pleasant roe,</hi> such as great men sometimes kept tame in their houses and played with. Desire no better diversion from severe study and business than the innocent and pleasant conversation of thy own wife; let her lie in thy bosom, as the poor man's ewe-lamb did in his (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.3">2 Sam. xii. 3</reference>), and do thou repose thy head in hers, and let that <hi type="italic">satisfy thee at all times;</hi> and seek not for pleasure in any other. "<hi type="italic">Err thou always in her love.</hi> If thou wilt suffer thy love to run into an excess, and wilt be dotingly fond of any body, let it be only of thy own wife, where there is least danger of exceeding." This is <hi type="italic">drinking waters,</hi> to quench the thirst of thy appetite, <hi type="italic">out of thy own cistern,</hi> and <hi type="italic">running waters,</hi> which are clear, and sweet, and wholesome, <hi type="italic">out of thy own well,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.15">v. 15. 1 Cor. vii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2-1Cor.7.3">3</reference>. <div eID="gen13458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> 4. Let him take delight in his children and look upon them with pleasure (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.16-Prov.5.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): "Look upon them as streams from thy own pure fountains" (the Jews are said to <hi type="italic">come forth out of the waters of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa. xlviii. 1</reference>), "so that they are parts of thyself, as the streams are of the fountain. Keep to thy own wife, and thou shalt have," (1.) "A numerous offspring, like <hi type="italic">rivers of water,</hi> which run in abundance, and they shall be dispersed abroad, matched into other families, whereas those that <hi type="italic">commit whoredom</hi> shall <hi type="italic">not increase,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.4.10">Hos. iv. 10</reference>. (2.) "A peculiar offspring, which shall be <hi type="italic">only thy own,</hi> whereas the children of whoredom, that are fathered upon thee, are, probably, not so, but, for aught thou knowest, are the offspring of strangers, and yet thou must keep them." (3.) "A creditable offspring, which are an honour to thee, and which thou mayest send abroad, and appear with, in the streets, whereas a spurious brood is thy disgrace, and that which thou art ashamed to own." In this matter, virtue has all the pleasure and honour in it; justly therefore it is called <hi type="italic">wisdom.</hi> <div eID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> 5. Let him then scorn the offer of forbidden pleasures when he is <hi type="italic">always ravished with the love</hi> of a faithful virtuous wife; let him consider what an absurdity it will be for him to be <hi type="italic">ravished with a strange woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.20">v. 20</reference>), to be in love with a filthy harlot, and <hi type="italic">embrace the bosom of a stranger,</hi> which, if he had any sense of honour or virtue, he would loathe the thoughts of. "Why wilt thou be so sottish, such an enemy to thyself, as to prefer puddle-water, and that poisoned too and stolen, before pure living waters out of thy own well?" Note, If the dictates of reason may be heard, the laws of virtue will be obeyed. <div eID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> II. "See the eye of God always upon thee and let his fear rule in thy heart," <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">v. 21</reference>. Those that live in this sin promise themselves secresy (<hi type="italic">the eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.15">Job xxiv. 15</reference>); but to what purpose, when it cannot be hidden from God? For, 1. He sees it. <hi type="italic">The ways of man,</hi> all his motions, all his actions, are <hi type="italic">before the eyes of the Lord,</hi> all the workings of the heart and all the outgoings of the life, that which is done ever so secretly and disguised ever so artfully. God sees it in a true light, and knows it with all its causes, circumstances, and consequences. He does not cast an eye upon men's ways now and then, but they are always actually in his view and under his inspection; and darest thou sin against God in his sight, and do that wickedness under his eye which thou durst not do in the presence of a man like thyself? 2. He will call the sinner to an account for it; for he not only sees, but <hi type="italic">ponders all his goings,</hi> judges concerning them, as one that will shortly judge the sinner for them. Every action is <hi type="italic">weighed,</hi> and shall be <hi type="italic">brought into judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">Eccl. xii. 14</reference>), which is a good reason why we should <hi type="italic">ponder the path of our feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">ch. iv. 26</reference>), and so <hi type="italic">judge ourselves</hi> that we <hi type="italic">may not be judged.</hi> <div eID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13462" type="x-p"/> III. "Foresee the certain ruin of those that go on still in their trespasses." Those that live in this sin promise themselves impunity, but they deceive themselves; their sin will find them out, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22-Prov.5.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. The apostle gives the sense of these verses in a few words. <reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">Heb. xiii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.</hi> 1. It is a sin which men with great difficulty shake off the power of. When the sinner is old and weak his lusts are strong and active, in <hi type="italic">calling to remembrance the days of his youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.19">Ezek. xxiii. 19</reference>. Thus <hi type="italic">his own iniquities</hi> having <hi type="italic">seized the wicked himself</hi> by his own consent, and he having voluntarily surrendered himself a captive to them, he is <hi type="italic">held in the cords of his own sins,</hi> and such full possession they have gained of him that he cannot extricate himself, but in the <hi type="italic">greatness of his folly</hi> (and what greater folly could there be than to yield himself a servant to such cruel task-masters?) he shall <hi type="italic">go astray,</hi> and wander endlessly. Uncleanness is a sin from which, when once men have plunged themselves into it, they very hardly and very rarely recover themselves. 2. It is a sin which, if it be not forsaken, men cannot possibly escape the punishment of; it will unavoidably be their ruin. As their own iniquities do arrest them in the reproaches of conscience and present rebukes (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">Jer. vii. 19</reference>), so their own iniquities shall arrest them and bind them over to the judgments of God. There needs no prison, no chains; they shall be <hi type="italic">holden in the cords of their own sins,</hi> as the fallen angels, being incurably wicked, are thereby <hi type="italic">reserved in chains of darkness.</hi> The sinner, who, having been <hi type="italic">often reproved, hardens his neck,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">die at length without instruction.</hi> Having had general warnings sufficient given him already, he shall have no particular warnings, but he shall die without seeing his danger beforehand, shall die because he would not receive instruction, but <hi type="italic">in the greatness of his folly</hi> would <hi type="italic">go astray;</hi> and so shall his doom be, he shall never find the way home again. Those that are so foolish as to choose the way of sin are justly left of God to themselves to go in it till they come to that destruction which it leads to, which is a good reason why we should guard with watchfulness and resolution against the allurements of the sensual appetite.  <chapter eID="Prov.5"/> <div eID="gen13462" type="x-p"/>

entries.c1fad5f4d6f1e50cc96ed144a21119bee08673d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7264"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Prov.5.1-Prov.5.23">Pr 5:1-23</reference>. A warning against the seductive arts of wicked women, enforced by considering the advantages of chastity, and the miserable end of the wicked.</title> <div sID="gen11212" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7264"/>1. This connection of wisdom and understanding is frequent (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.2">Pr 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">3:7</reference>); the first denotes the use of wise means for wise ends; the other, the exercise of a proper discrimination in their discovery. <div eID="gen11212" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cec75a10638367cd7377294ad25f8bbb494027b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7265"/><div sID="gen11213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7265"/><hi type="bold">2. regard--</hi>or, "observe."<div eID="gen11213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep--</hi>preserve constantly. <div eID="gen11214" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a99320cb5b91c546cbe0dd9cff6926b32fd179e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7266"/><div sID="gen11215" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7266"/>3. (Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pr 2:16</reference>). Her enticing promises are deceitful. <div eID="gen11215" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e08a4181b63721d4c3cf1c1b933545fbefd0da9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7267"/><div sID="gen11216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7267"/><hi type="bold">4. her end--</hi>literally, "her future," in sense of reward, what follows (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Psa 37:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">73:17</reference>). Its nature is evinced by the use of figures, opposite those of <reference osisRef="Prov.5.3">Pr 5:3</reference>. The physical and moral suffering of the deluded profligate are notoriously terrible. <div eID="gen11216" type="x-p"/>
entries.0400cba697185a2168b6a6e91823273c5bb475a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7268"/><div sID="gen11217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7268"/><hi type="bold">5. feet ... , steps--</hi>that is, course of life ends in death. <div eID="gen11217" type="x-p"/>
entries.e881f9ae30eb89f1570b03dab0d90c1a0759f875: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7269"/><div sID="gen11218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7269"/><hi type="bold">6. her ways ... know--</hi>Some prefer, "that she may not ponder the path of life," &c.; but perhaps a better sense is, "her ways are varied, so as to prevent your knowledge of her true character, and so of true happiness." <div eID="gen11218" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee0941123405f01203a44dc88c21047a7e58ca4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7270"/><div sID="gen11219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7270"/>8-9. Avoid the slightest temptation. <div eID="gen11219" type="x-p"/>
entries.aea1c99e2f40d16c5d2c7380c46d2b8070d856da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7272"/><div sID="gen11223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7272"/><hi type="bold">10. wealth--</hi>literally, "strength," or the result of it.<div eID="gen11223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labours--</hi>the fruit of thy painful exertions (<reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Psa 127:2</reference>). There may be a reference to slavery, a commuted punishment for death due the adulterer (<reference osisRef="Deut.22.22">De 22:22</reference>). <div eID="gen11224" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc2af94d523eefd891e33549e31243e97736a9c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7273"/><div sID="gen11225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7273"/><hi type="bold">11. at the last--</hi>the end, or reward (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.5.4">Pr 5:4</reference>).<div eID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mourn--</hi>roar in pain.<div eID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh and ... body--</hi>the whole person under incurable disease. <div eID="gen11227" type="x-p"/>
entries.93e7f071cd582f478ece3b7d5cdcd1d7a35c85c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7274"/><div sID="gen11228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7274"/>12-14. The ruined sinner vainly laments his neglect of warning and his sad fate in being brought to public disgrace. <div eID="gen11228" type="x-p"/>
entries.b53ac2fa50131b98bf4275b1284f6d51acaaf71e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7276"/><div sID="gen11230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7276"/>15-20. By figures, in which well, cistern, and fountain [Pr 5:15, 18] represent the wife, and rivers of waters [Pr 5:16] the children, men are exhorted to constancy and satisfaction in lawful conjugal enjoyments. In <reference osisRef="Prov.5.16">Pr 5:16</reference>, fountains (in the plural) rather denote the produce or waters of a spring, literally, "what is from a spring," and corresponds with "rivers of waters." <div eID="gen11230" type="x-p"/>
entries.c11e037869b1d21823a07adcee256f5415c44a49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7280"/><div sID="gen11236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7280"/>21. The reason, God's eye is on you, <div eID="gen11236" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bce7e3e3d91c0aab0086864cdab34f8d00ea85a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7281"/><div sID="gen11237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7281"/>22-23. and He will cause sin to bring its punishment. <div eID="gen11237" type="x-p"/>

entries.7d3c675a122c8f3220895af68c0638c26be82fdf: <div eID="gen23855" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23856" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23857" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23857" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23856" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23858" type="x-p"/> Farther exhortations to acquire wisdom, <reference osisRef="Pro.5.1">Pro 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference>. The character of a loose woman, and the ruinous consequences of attachment to such, <reference osisRef="Pro.5.3-Pro.5.14">Pro 5:3-14</reference>. Exhortations to chastity and moderation, <reference osisRef="Pro.5.15-Pro.5.21">Pro 5:15-21</reference>. The miserable end of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Pro.5.22">Pro 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.5.23">Pro 5:23</reference>. <div eID="gen23858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23859" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23860" type="x-p"/> Attend unto my wisdom - Take the following lessons from my own experience.
entries.716549b2c5fd0417b39182fd70de3a6a2d52e7ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23861" type="x-p"/> The lips of a strange woman - One that is not thy own, whether Jewess or heathen. <div eID="gen23861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23862" type="x-p"/> Drop as a honey-comb - She uses the most deceitful, flattering, and alluring speeches: as the droppings of the honey out of the comb are the sweetest of all.
entries.edab0512f01bed883f942a468756dc5abf5a971c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23863" type="x-p"/> Bitter as wormwood - כלענה Kelanah, like the detestable herb wormwood, or something analogous to it: something as excessive in its bitterness, as honey is in its sweetness.
entries.e1f1ea38270ae36f217b3d85a91063d93562c1ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23864" type="x-p"/> Her feet go down to death - She first, like a serpent, infuses her poison, by which the whole constitution of her paramour is infected, which soon or late brings on death. <div eID="gen23864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23865" type="x-p"/> Her steps take hold on hell - First, the death of the body; and then the damnation of the soul. These are the tendencies of connections with such women.
entries.2b79827a745171b04208469bfbdac80b34a995a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23866" type="x-p"/> Lest thou shouldest ponder - To prevent thee from reflecting on thy present conduct, and its consequences, her ways are moveable - she continually varies her allurements. <div eID="gen23866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23867" type="x-p"/> Thou canst not know them - It is impossible to conceive all her tricks and wiles: to learn these in all their varieties, is a part of the science first taught in that infernal trade.
entries.6330e3ff8146a2e916aad8d50eb045e60af71ba3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23868" type="x-p"/> Hear me - O ye children - בנים banim, sons, young men in general: for these are the most likely to be deceived and led astray.
entries.8ad6e9b30d3b06a9e43bb5ff68f01f4835486ef5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23869" type="x-p"/> Come not nigh the door of her house - Where there are generally such exhibitions as have a natural tendency to excite impure thoughts, and irregular passions.
entries.3e70e8da7003609d0b8f2aaa2b8a71ca0eed12de: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23870" type="x-p"/> Lest thou give thine honor - The character of a debauchee is universally detested: by this, even those of noble blood lose their honor and respect. <div eID="gen23870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23871" type="x-p"/> Thy years unto the cruel - Though all the blandishments of love dwell on the tongue, and the excess of fondness appear in the whole demeanor of the harlot and the prostitute; yet cruelty has its throne in their hearts; and they will rob and murder (when it appears to answer their ends) those who give their strength, their wealth, and their years to them. The unfaithful wife has often murdered her own husband for the sake of her paramour, and has given him over to justice in order to save herself. Murders have often taken place in brothels, as well as robberies; for the vice of prostitution is one of the parents of cruelty.
entries.e6fdad25a07e647e5c0389efb01275795eb664dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen23871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23872" type="x-p"/> When thy flesh and thy body are consumed - The word שאר shear, which we render body, signifies properly the remains, residue, or remnant of a thing: and is applied here to denote the breathing carcass, putrid with the concomitant disease of debauchery: a public reproach which the justice of God entails on this species of iniquity. The mourning here spoken of is of the most excessive kind: the word נהם naham is often applied to the growling of a lion, and the hoarse incessant murmuring of the sea. In the line of my duty, I have been often called to attend the death-bed of such persons, where groans and shrieks were incessant through the jaculating pains in their bones and flesh. Whoever has witnessed a closing scene like this will at once perceive with what force and propriety the wise man speaks. And How have I hated instruction, and despised the voice of my teachers! is the unavailing cry in that terrific time. Reader, whosoever thou art, lay these things to heart. Do not enter into their sin: once entered, thy return is nearly hopeless.
entries.7b9b94c200a12083f1df6132ecfcb61321b9c75c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23873" type="x-p"/> I was almost in all evil - This vice, like a whirlpool, sweeps all others into its vortex. <div eID="gen23873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23874" type="x-p"/> In the midst of the congregation and assembly - In the mydel of the Curche and of the Synagoge - Old MS. Bible. Such persons, however sacred the place, carry about with them eyes full of adultery, which cannot cease from sin.
entries.e9ff23e4f78a2046930500344ffe55f23d574135: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23875" type="x-p"/> Drink waters out of thine own cistern - Be satisfied with thy own wife; and let the wife see that she reverence her husband; and not tempt him by inattention or unkindness to seek elsewhere what he has a right to expect, but cannot find, at home.
entries.c69bdf9b256611cfa7110ad54b00fd9a0e65259f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen23875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23876" type="x-p"/> Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad - Let thy children lawfully begotten be numerous.
entries.c9de22e016c82e7d8d731cffe2214a55bb333bf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen23876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23877" type="x-p"/> Let them be only thine own - The off-spring of a legitimate connection; a bastard brood, however numerous, is no credit to any man.
entries.4d9c7bd45fe7ded02d98cfe4b097e9492c9a8b89: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen23877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23878" type="x-p"/> Let thy fountain be blessed - יהי מקורך ברוך yehi mekorecha baruch. Sit vena tua benedicta. Thy vein; that which carries off streams from the fountain of animal life, in order to disperse them abroad, and through the streets. How delicate and correct is the allusion here! But anatomical allusions must not be pressed into detail in a commentary on Scripture.
entries.79fc3fceff94aae3e2a4d36f8737cfea408af18a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen23878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23879" type="x-p"/> The loving hind and pleasant roe - By אילת aiyeleth, the deer; by יעלה yaalah, the ibex or mountain goat, may be meant. <div eID="gen23879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23880" type="x-p"/> Let her breasts satisfy thee - As the infant is satisfied with the breasts of its mother; so shouldst thou be with the wife of thy youth.
entries.8304e12dcd7dd28dc227e3d69f4e9dd893c4587e: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen23880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23881" type="x-p"/> For the ways of a man - Whether they are public or private, God sees all the steps thou takest in life.
entries.7ddd9787e091ce00a5cfd1c2d9e79022444db8f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen23881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23882" type="x-p"/> He shall be holden with the cords of his sins - Most people who follow unlawful pleasures, think they can give them up whenever they please; but sin repeated becomes customary; custom soon engenders habit; and habit in the end assumes the form of necessity; the man becomes bound with his own cords, and so is led captive by the devil at his will.
entries.d45a4793f1039b96d16001587b554f5c800dfebf: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen23882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23883" type="x-p"/> He shall die without instruction - This is most likely, and it is a general case; but even these may repent and live.  <chapter eID="Prov.5"/> <div eID="gen23883" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e93379608304623cb065c8dc859190c74a1fd06: <reference osisRef="Prov.5.1-Prov.5.6">Pro 5:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen10689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10690" type="x-p"/> Here a fourth rule of life follows the three already given, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.24">Pro 4:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.25">Pro 4:25</reference>, Pro 4:26-27 : 1 My son, attend unto my wisdom,    And incline thine ear to my prudence, 2 To observe discretion,    And that thy lips preserve knowledge. 3 For the lips of the adulteress distil honey,    And smoother than oil is her mouth; 4 But her end is bitter like wormwood,    Sharper than a two-edged sword. 5 Her feet go down to death,    Her steps cleave to Hades. 6 She is far removed from entering the way of life,    Her steps wander without her observing it. <div eID="gen10690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10691" type="x-p"/> Wisdom and understanding increase with the age of those who earnestly seek after them. It is the father of the youth who here requests a willing ear to his wisdom of life, gained in the way of many years’ experience and observation. In <reference osisRef="Prov.5.2">Pro 5:2</reference> the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. of the object is continued in the <hi type="italic">finitum</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.2.2">Pro 2:2</reference>, Pro 2:8. מזמּות (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on its etymon under <reference osisRef="Prov.1.4">Pro 1:4</reference>) are plans, projects, designs, for the most part in a bad sense, intrigues and artifices (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.24.8">Pro 24:8</reference>), but also used of well-considered resolutions toward what is good, and hence of the purposes of God, Jer 23:20. This noble sense of the word מזמּה, with its plur., is peculiar to the introductory portion (chap. 1-9) of the Book of Proverbs. The plur. means here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.8.12">Pro 8:12</reference> (placing itself with חכמות and תּבוּנות, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 68) the reflection and deliberation which is the presupposition of well-considered action, and שׁמר is thus not otherwise than at <reference osisRef="Prov.19.8">Pro 19:8</reference>, and everywhere so meant, where it has that which is obligatory as its object: the youth is summoned to careful observation and persevering exemplification of the <hi type="italic">quidquid agas, prudenter agas et respice finem</hi>. In 2b the <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> forbids the genitive connection of the two words דּעתו שׂפתיך; we translate: <hi type="italic">et ut scientiam labia tua tueantur</hi>. Lips which preserve knowledge are such as permit nothing to escape from them (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>) which proceeds not from the knowledge of God, and in Him of that which is good and right, and aims at the working out of this knowledge; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Köhler on Mal 2:7. שׂפתיך (from שׂפה, Arab. shafat, edge, lip, properly that against which one rubs, and that which rubs itself) is fem., but the usage of the language presents the word in two genders (cf. 3a with <reference osisRef="Prov.26.23">Pro 26:23</reference>). Regarding the pausal ינצרוּ for יצּרוּ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Mal 3:1; Mal 2:11. The lips which distil the honey of enticement stand opposite to the lips which distil knowledge; the object of the admonition is to furnish a protection against the honey-lips.
entries.6b5f4b4211e16b8429bde841b82dfc32046640eb: <reference osisRef="Prov.5.7-Prov.5.11">Pro 5:7-11</reference> <div eID="gen10693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10694" type="x-p"/> The eighth discourse springs out of the conclusion of the seventh, and connects itself by its reflective מעליה so closely with it that it appears as its continuation; but the new beginning and its contents included in it, referring only to social life, secures its relative independence. The poet derives the warning against intercourse with the adulteress from the preceding discourse, and grounds it on the destructive consequences. 7 And now, ye sons, hearken unto me,    And depart not from the words of my mouth. 8 Hold thy path far from her neighbourhood,    And come not to the door of her house! 9 That thou mayest not give the freshness of thy youth to another,    Nor thy years to the cruel one; 10 That strangers may not sate themselves with thy possessions,    And the fruit of thy toils come into the house of a stranger, 11 And thou groanest at the end,    When thy flesh and thy body are consumed. <div eID="gen10694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10695" type="x-p"/> Neither here nor in the further stages of this discourse is there any reference to the criminal punishment inflicted on the adulterer, which, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.20.10">Lev 20:10</reference>, consisted in death, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.40">Eze 16:40</reference>, cf. John. <reference osisRef="Prov.8.5">Pro 8:5</reference>, in stoning, and according to a later traditional law, in strangulation (חנק). Ewald finds in <reference osisRef="Prov.5.14">Pro 5:14</reference> a play on this punishment of adultery prescribed by law, and reads from Pro 5:9. that the adulterer who is caught by the injured husband was reduced to the state of a slave, and was usually deprived of his manhood. But that any one should find pleasure in making the destroyer of his wife his slave is a far-fetched idea, and neither the law nor the history of Israel contains any evidence for this punishment by slavery or the mutilation of the adulterer, for which Ewald refers to Grimm’s <hi type="italic">Deutsche Rechtsaltertümer</hi>. The figure which is here sketched by the poet is very different. He who goes into the net of the wanton woman loses his health and his goods. She stands not alone, but has her party with her, who wholly plunder the simpleton who goes into her trap. Nowhere is there any reference to the husband of the adulteress. The poet does not at all think on a married woman. And the word chosen directs our attention rather to a foreigner than to an Israelitish woman, although the author may look upon harlotry as such as heathenish rather than Israelitish, and designate it accordingly. The party of those who make prostitutes of themselves consists of their relations and their older favourites, the companions of their gain, who being in league with her exhaust the life-strength and the resources of the befooled youth (Fl.). This discourse begins with ועתּה, for it is connected by this concluding application (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.7.24">Pro 7:24</reference>) with the preceding.
entries.b385ebb0d834874dc2720ebd848aa207734b85c6: <reference osisRef="Prov.5.12-Prov.5.14">Pro 5:12-14</reference> <div eID="gen10698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10699" type="x-p"/> The poet now tells those whom he warns to hear how the voluptuary, looking back on his life-course, passes sentence against himself. 12 And thou sayest, “Why have I then hated correction,      And my heart despised instruction! 13 And I have not listened to the voice of my teachers,      Nor lent mine ear to my instructors? 14 I had almost fallen into every vice      In the midst of the assembly and the congregation!” <div eID="gen10699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10700" type="x-p"/> The question 12a (here more an exclamation than a question) is the combination of two: How has it become possible for me? How could it ever come to it that.... Thus also one says in Arab.: Kyf f'alat hadhâ (Fl.). The regimen of איך in 12b is becoming faint, and in 13b has disappeared. The <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> נאץ (as <reference osisRef="Prov.1.30">Pro 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.15.5">Pro 15:5</reference>) signifies to despise; the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> intensively, to contemn and reject (R. נץ, <hi type="italic">pungere</hi>).
entries.b7fa2a418bbcfe8e25a28d7cae7eeec57c53c31d: <reference osisRef="Prov.5.15-Prov.5.17">Pro 5:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen10700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10701" type="x-p"/> The commendation of true conjugal love in the form of an invitation to a participation in it, is now presented along with the warning against non-conjugal intercourse, heightened by a reference to its evil consequences. 15 Drink water from thine own cistern,      And flowing streams from thine own fountain. 16 Shall thy streams flow abroad,      The water-brooks in the streets! 17 Let them belong to thyself alone,      And not to strangers with thee. <div eID="gen10701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10702" type="x-p"/> One drinks water to quench his thirst; here drinking is a figure of the satisfaction of conjugal love, of which Paul says, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.9">1Co 7:9</reference>, κρεῖσσόν ἐστι γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι, and this comes into view here, in conformity with the prevailing character of the O.T., only as a created inborn natural impulse, without reference to the poisoning of it by sin, which also within the sphere of married life makes government, moderation, and restraint a duty. Warning against this degeneracy of the natural impulse to the πάθος ἐπιθυμίας authorized within divinely prescribed limits, the apostle calls the wife of any one τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος (cf. 1Pe 3:7). So here the wife, who is his by covenant (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pro 2:17</reference>), is called “cistern” (בור)<note placement="foot">The lxx translate ἀπὸ σῶν ἀγγείων, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, מכּוריך (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lagarde).</note> and “fountain” (בּאר) of the husband to whom she is married. The figure corresponds to the sexual nature of the wife, the expression for which is נקבה; but <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1">Isa 51:1</reference> holds to the natural side of the figure, for according to it the wife is a pit, and the children are brought out of it into the light of day. Aben-Ezra on <reference osisRef="Lev.11.36">Lev 11:36</reference> rightly distinguishes between בור and באר: the former catches the rain, the latter wells out from within. In the former, as Rashi in <hi type="italic">Erubin</hi> ii. 4 remarks, there are מים מכונסים, in the latter חיים מים. The post-biblical Hebrew observes this distinction less closely (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi’s <hi type="italic">Book of Roots</hi>), but the biblical throughout; so far the Kerı̂, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">Jer 6:7</reference>, rightly changes בור into the form בּיר, corresponding to the Arab. byar. Therefore בור is the cistern, for the making of which חצב, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jer 2:13</reference>, and באר the well, for the formation of which חפר, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.30">Gen 21:30</reference>, and כרה, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.25">Gen 26:25</reference>, are the respective words usually employed (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Malbim, <hi type="italic">Sifra</hi> 117b). The poet shows that he also is aware of this distinction, for he calls the water which one drinks from the בור by the name מים, but on the other hand that out of the באר by the name נוזלים, running waters, <hi type="italic">fluenta</hi>; by this we are at once reminded of Sol 4:15, cf. 12. The בור offers only stagnant water (according to the Sohar, the בור has no water of its own, but only that which is received into it), although coming down into it from above; but the באר has living water, which wells up out of its interior (מתּוך, 15b, intentionally for the mere מן), and is fresh as the streams from Lebanon (נזל, properly <hi type="italic">labi</hi>, to run down, cf. אזל, <hi type="italic">placide ire</hi>, and generally <hi type="italic">ire</hi>; Arab. zâl, <hi type="italic">loco cedere, desinere</hi>; Arab. zll, IV, to cause to glide back, <hi type="italic">deglutire</hi>, of the gourmand). What a valuable possession a well of water is for nomads the history of the patriarchs makes evident, and a cistern is one of the most valuable possessions belonging to every well-furnished house. The figure of the cistern is here surpassed by that of the fountain, but both refer to the seeking and finding satisfaction (cf. the opposite passage, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.27">Pro 23:27</reference>) with the wife, and that, as the expressive possessive suffixes denote, with his legitimate wife.
entries.6c0132c3399356d961908b4d33ff6cd6658f7217: <reference osisRef="Prov.5.18-Prov.5.20">Pro 5:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen10705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10706" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Prov.5.18">Pro 5:18</reference> is introduced anew the praise of conjugal love. These three verses, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.18-Prov.5.21">Pro 5:18-21</reference>, have the same course of thought as <reference osisRef="Prov.5.15">Pro 5:15</reference>-17. 18 Let thy fountain be blessed,      And rejoice in the wife of thy youth. 19 The lovely hind and the graceful gazelle -      May her bosom always charm thee;      In her love mayest thou delight thyself evermore. 20 But why wilt thou be fascinated with a stranger,      And embrace the bosom of a foreign woman? <div eID="gen10706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10707" type="x-p"/> Like בור and באר, מקור is also a figure of the wife; the root-word is קוּר, from קר, כר, the meanings of which, to dig and make round, come together in the primary conception of the round digging out or boring out, not קוּר = קרר, the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of which means (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">Jer 6:7</reference>) to well out cold (water). It is the fountain of the birth that is meant (cf. מקור of the female ערוה, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.18">Lev 20:18</reference>), not the procreation (lxx, ἡ σὴ φλέψ, viz., φλὲψ γονίμη); the blessing wished for by him is the blessing of children, which בּרוּך so much the more distinctly denotes if בּרך, Arab. barak, means to spread out, and בּרך thus to cause a spreading out. The מן, 18b, explains itself from the idea of drawing (water), given with the figure of a fountain; the word בּאשׁת found in certain codices is, on the contrary, prosaic (Fl.). Whilst שׂמח מן is found elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.20">Ecc 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.27">2Ch 20:27</reference>) as meaning almost the same as שׂמח בּ; the former means rejoicing from some place, the latter in something. In the genitive connection, “wife of thy youth” (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.17">Pro 2:17</reference>), both of these significations lie: thy youthful wife, and she who was chosen by thee in thy youth, according as we refer the suffix to the whole idea or only to the second member of the chain of words.
entries.da1e8aa9c99f08003f232332a9e1e87d1f1c133c: <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21-Prov.5.23">Pro 5:21-23</reference> <div eID="gen10709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10710" type="x-p"/> That the intercourse of the sexes out of the married relationship is the commencement of the ruin of a fool is now proved. 21 For the ways of every one are before the eyes of Jahve,      And all his paths He marketh out. 22 His own sins lay hold of him, the evil-doer,      And in the bands of his sins is he held fast. 23 He dies for the want of correction,      And in the fulness of his folly he staggers to ruin. <div eID="gen10710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10711" type="x-p"/> It is unnecessary to interpret נכח as an adverbial accusative: straight before Jahve’s eyes; it may be the nominative of the predicate; the ways of man (for אישׁ is here an individual, whether man or woman) are an object (properly, fixing) of the eyes of Jahve. With this the thought would suitably connect itself: <hi type="italic">et onmes orbitas ejus ad amussim examinat</hi>; but פּלּס, as the denom. of פּלס, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.3">Psa 58:3</reference>, is not connected with all the places where the verb is united with the obj. of the way, and <reference osisRef="Ps.78.50">Psa 78:50</reference> shows that it has there the meaning to break though, to open a way (from פל, to split, cf. Talmudic מפלּשׁ, opened, accessible, from פלשׁ, Syriac pelaa, <hi type="italic">perfodere, fodiendo viam, aditum sibi aperire</hi>). The opening of the way is here not, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.26.7">Isa 26:7</reference>, conceived of as the setting aside of the hindrances in the way of him who walks, but generally as making walking in the way possible: man can take no step in any direction without God; and that not only does not exempt him from moral responsibility, but the consciousness of this is rather for the first time rightly quickened by the consciousness of being encompassed on every side by the knowledge and the power of God. The dissuasion of <reference osisRef="Prov.5.20">Pro 5:20</reference> is thus in <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">Pro 5:21</reference> grounded in the fact, that man at every stage and step of his journey is observed and encompassed by God: it is impossible for him to escape from the knowledge of God or from dependence on Him. Thus opening all the paths of man, He has also appointed to the way of sin the punishment with which it corrects itself: “his sins lay hold of him, the evil-doer.” The suffix  יו does not refer to אישׁ of <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">Pro 5:21</reference>, where every one without exception and without distinction is meant, but it relates to the obj. following, the evil-doer, namely, as the explanatory permutative annexed to the “him” according to the scheme, <reference osisRef="Exod.2.6">Exo 2:6</reference>; the permutative is distinguished from the apposition by this, that the latter is a forethought explanation which heightens the understanding of the subject, while the former is an explanation afterwards brought in which guards against a misunderstanding. The same construction, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.13">Pro 14:13</reference>, belonging to the <hi type="italic">syntaxis ornata</hi> in the old Hebrew, has become common in the Aramaic and in the modern Hebrew. Instead of ילכּדוּהוּ (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">Pro 5:22</reference>), the poet uses poetically ילכּדנו; the interposed נ may belong to the emphatic ground-form ילכּדוּן, but is epenthetic if one compares forms such as קבנו (R. קב), Num 23:13 (cf. p. 73). The חמּאתו governed by חבלי, <hi type="italic">laquei</hi> (חבלי, <hi type="italic">tormina</hi>), is either <hi type="italic">gen. exeg</hi>.: bands which consist in his sin, or <hi type="italic">gen. subj</hi>.: bands which his sin unites, or better, gen. possess.: bands which his sin brings with it. By these bands he will be held fast, and so will die: he (הוּא referring to the person described) will die in insubordination (Symm. δι ̓ ἀπαιδευσίαν), or better, since אין and רב are placed in contrast: in want of correction. With the ישׁגּה (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.23">Pro 5:23</reference>), repeated purposely from <reference osisRef="Prov.5.20">Pro 5:20</reference>, there is connected the idea of the overthrow which is certain to overtake the infatuated man. In <reference osisRef="Prov.5.20">Pro 5:20</reference> the sense of moral error began already to connect itself with this verb. אוּלת is the right name of unrestrained lust of the flesh. אולת is connected with אוּל, the belly; אול, Arab. âl, to draw together, to condense, to thicken (<hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi>, p. 424). <hi type="italic">Dummheit</hi> (stupidity) and the Old-Norse <hi type="italic">dumba</hi>, darkness, are in their roots related to each other. Also in the Semitic the words for blackness and darkness are derived from roots meaning condensation. אויל is the mind made thick, darkened, and become like crude matter.  <chapter eID="Prov.5"/> <div eID="gen10711" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. V.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. MY son, attend unto my wisdom, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> bow thine ear to my understanding.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. That thou maist regard <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>keep, i. e.</ns0:hi> hold fast, as it is in the next clause.</ns0:note> discretion <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual Wisdom for the conduct of thy Life, as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 4. and elsewhere in this Book.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thy lips may keep knowledge <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That by wise and pious discourses thou maist preserve and improve thy Wisdom for thine own and others good.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2. 16. & 6. 24.</ns0:note> For <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It concerns thee to get, and to use discretion, that thou maist be able to resist and repel those manifold Temptations to which thou art exposed.</ns0:note> the lips of a strange woman drop <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> an hony-comb <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Her words and discourses are sweet, and charming, and prevalent.</ns0:note>, and her <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>palate.</ns0:hi> oil.</ns0:note> mouth <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> smoother than</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 But her end is bitter as wormwood <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Her design, and the effect of that lewdness to which she en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticeth men, is the sinners destruction.</ns0:note>, sharp as a two-edged Sword.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7. 27.</ns0:note> Her feet <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Her course or manner of Life.</ns0:note> go down to death: her steps take hold on hell.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Lest thou shouldst ponder the path of life <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To prevent thy serious consideration of the way and manner of rescuing thy self from this deadly course of Life.</ns0:note>, her ways are moveable <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Various and changeable. She transforms her self into several shapes to accom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />modate her self to the humours of her Lovers, and hath a Thou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sand Arts and Deceits to enshare them, and hold them fast.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou canst not know <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Thou canst not discover all her subtil practices, and much less deliver thy self from them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. Hear me now therefore, O ye Children, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />part not from the words of my mouth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7. 7, 8, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her House <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Lest thine eyes affect thine Heart, and her allurements pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vail over thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Lest thou give thine honour <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Thy Dignity and Reputation, the strength and vigour of thy Body and Mind, which is an honour to a man, and which are commonly wasted by Adulterous practices.</ns0:note> unto others <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Unto Whores and their Husbands and Children and Friends.</ns0:note>, and thy years <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The flower of thine age, thy youthful years.</ns0:note> unto the cruel <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To the Harlot, who though she pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tends ardent Love and kindness to thee, yet in truth is one of the most cruel Creatures in the World, wasting thy Estate and Body without the least pity, and then casting thee off with scorn and contempt, and when her Interest requires it, taking away thy ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry life, of which there are enumerable examples, and damning thy Soul for ever.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Lest strangers <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Not onely the strange women themselves, but Bawds, Panders, and other Adulterers, who are in league with them.</ns0:note> be filled with <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> thy strength.</ns0:note> thy wealth, and thy labours <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Wealth gotten by thy labours.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> in the house of a stranger,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. And thou mourn at the last <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Bitterly bewail thy own madness and misery when it is too late.</ns0:note>, when thy flesh, and thy body <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Thy Flesh, even thy Body; the particle, <ns0:hi>and,</ns0:hi> being put exposi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tively.</ns0:note> are consumed <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">By those manifold diseases which filthy and inordinate Lusts bring upon the Body, of which Physicians give a very large and sad Catalogue, and the Bodies of many Adulterers give full</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. And say, how have I hated instruction <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Oh what a mad beast have I been to hate and sleight the fair warnings which were given me, and against mine own knowledg, to run headlong into this pit of destruction! Which are not the words of a true penitent mourning for, and turning from his sin, but only of a man who is grieved for the sad effects of his delightful Lusts, and tormented with the horrour of his own guilty Consci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence.</ns0:note>, and my heart despised reproof <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I did with my whole Heart abhor all admonitions.</ns0:note>!</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. And have not obeyed the voice of my Teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of my Parents and Friends, and Ministers, who faithfully and seasonably informed me of those mischiefs and miseries which now I feel.</ns0:note>, nor enclined mine ear to them that instructed me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. I was almost in all evil <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Oh what a miserable man am I! There is scarce any misery in respect of Estate, or Body, or Soul, into which I am not already plunged. The words also are and may well be rendred thus, <ns0:hi>In a mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment I am come into all evil.</ns0:hi> In how little a time, and for what short and momentany pleasures am I now come into extream and reme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diless misery! I who designed and expected to enjoy my Lusts with secrecy, and impunity, am now made a publick example and shameful spectacle to all men, and that in the Congregation of <ns0:hi>Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael,</ns0:hi> where I was taught better things, and where such Actions are most infamous and hateful.</ns0:note>, in the midst of the congregation and Assembly <ns0:hi>b.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:521" />15. Drink Waters out of thine own cistern; and running waters out of thine own well <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This Metaphor contained here, and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 16, 17, 18. is to be understood, either 1. of the free and lawful use of a mans estate, both for his own comfort, and for the good of others. Or rather 2. of the honest use of Matrimony, as the proper Remedy against these filthy practices. This best suits with the whole context both foregoing and following: and thus it is explained in the end of <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18. So the sense is, Content thy self with those delights which God alloweth thee, with the sober use of the Marriage-Bed. Why shouldst thou ramble hither and thither, trespassing against God and men, to steal their Waters which thou mightst freely take out of thine own Cistern or Well. The ground of the Metaphor is this, that waters were scarce and precious in those Countries, and therefore men used to make Cisterns & Wells for their own private use. And the same Metaphor of <ns0:hi>Waters,</ns0:hi> and of a <ns0:hi>Pit,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Well</ns0:hi> is ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plied to things of this nature elsewhere, as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 23. 27. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 48. 1. & 51. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. Let thy fountains <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thy Children proceeding from thy Wife, called <ns0:hi>thy fountain,</ns0:hi> v. 18. and from thy self, as the Israelites are said to come from the <ns0:hi>Fountain of</ns0:hi> Israel, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 28. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68. 26. Compare <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 51. 1. And <ns0:hi>Fountains</ns0:hi> are here put for <ns0:hi>Rivers</ns0:hi> flowing from them, as it is explained in the next clause, and as it is <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 104. 10. by a Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tonymy of the Cause for the Effect. And this title may be the more fitly given to Children, because as they are Rivers in respect of their Parents, so when they grow up, they also become Foun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains to their Children.</ns0:note> be dispersed abroad <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">They shall be multiplied, and in due time appear abroad in the World to thy Comfort and Honour, and for the good of others: whereas Whores are commonly barren, and men are ashamed to own the Children of Whoredom.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> rivers of Waters in the streets.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Let them be only thine own, and not strangers with thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Hereby thou mayest be secured, that thou dost not father and leave thine Estate to other mens Children, whereas the Parents of Harlots Children are common or uncertain.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. Let thy fountain <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Thy Wife, as the next clause explains it.</ns0:note> be blessed <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">She shall be blessed with Children, for Barrenness was esteemed a curse and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proach, especially among the Israelites. Or rather, she shall be a Blessing and a Comfort to thee, as it follows, and not a Curse and a Snare, as an Harlot will be.</ns0:note>: and rejoice with the wife <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Seek not to Harlots for that de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />light which God alloweth thee to take with thy Wife.
